questions.prompt: What does recall@10 of 0.9 for an ANN index, measured against exact search, mean?
options: 90% of queries return results in under 10 ms
On average 9 of the true 10 nearest neighbours are returned
90% of returned documents are relevant to users
The index uses 90% less memory
questions.explanation: Recall@k against exact search is the overlap between the ANN top k and the brute-force top k. It says nothing about latency, memory or whether users find the results relevant.

questions.prompt: If all vectors are normalised to unit length, ranking by inner product gives the same order as ranking by cosine similarity.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For unit vectors the inner product equals the cosine, so the orders are identical. This is why many systems normalise and use inner product.

questions.prompt: In an IVF index, what does nprobe control?
options: The number of k-means cells scanned per query
The number of links per graph node
The bytes per compressed sub-vector
How many replicas store the data
questions.explanation: IVF scans only the lists of the nprobe nearest centroids. Links per node is HNSW's M, and bytes per code relates to product quantization.

questions.prompt: Which statements about HNSW are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Raising ef_search usually increases recall and latency
M is set when the index is built
Search starts at the dense bottom layer and climbs up
The graph is normally held in memory
questions.explanation: ef_search is a query-time recall dial, M is a build parameter and HNSW graphs are memory-resident. Search starts at the sparse top layer and descends, so the third option is reversed.

questions.prompt: A 768-dimensional float32 vector is compressed with product quantization using m = 96 sub-vectors and 256-centroid codebooks. How many bytes does each code take?
questions.code:
dims, m, codebook = 768, 96, 256
import math
print(m * math.ceil(math.log2(codebook) / 8))
questions.explanation: Each sub-vector is stored as the index of one of 256 centroids, which fits in one byte, so 96 sub-vectors take 96 bytes. 3072 is the uncompressed float32 size.

questions.prompt: A legal search tool filters by client_id after taking the ANN top 20. Small clients often see zero results. What is the best fix?
options: Raise k to 1,000 for every query
Use filtered search that applies client_id during traversal, with an indexed payload field
Switch the metric to Euclidean
Shard the index by embedding dimension
questions.explanation: Post-filtering fails for selective filters. Filtering during search guarantees k matches if they exist. A huge k only lowers the odds of failure and costs latency for everyone.

questions.prompt: After upgrading the embedding model, new documents are embedded with the new model and old ones are left untouched. Relevance collapses for old documents. Why?
options: HNSW cannot store more than one model's vectors
Vectors from different models live in different spaces and are not comparable, so old documents must be re-embedded
The new model uses a larger ef_search
Metadata filters were dropped during the upgrade
questions.explanation: Similarity is only meaningful within one embedding space. Queries now use the new model, so old vectors are effectively random relative to them. The fix is a full re-embed, usually into a new index with a cutover.

questions.prompt: You must pick between pgvector and a dedicated vector database for 2 million chunks with per-user permission filters, and you already run Postgres. What is the most defensible process?
options: Pick whichever vendor benchmark shows the highest QPS
Prototype both on your own data and filters, measure recall@k against exact search, p95 latency and operational fit, then decide
Always pick a dedicated vector database above one million vectors
Pick pgvector because SQL is familiar, without measuring
questions.explanation: Published benchmarks rarely match your data, filters and hardware. Measuring recall, latency and operational cost on your own workload is the defensible choice; blanket rules in either direction are not.

coding.title: Brute-force cosine top-k
coding.prompt:
Write `top_k(query, vectors, k)` where `vectors` is a dict of id to list of floats. Return the ids of the `k` most cosine-similar vectors, highest first. Break ties by id ascending. Ignore zero-length vectors.

Example: `top_k([1, 0], {'a': [1, 0], 'b': [0, 1], 'c': [1, 1]}, 2)` returns `['a', 'c']`.
coding.explanation: Cosine divides the dot product by both lengths, so magnitude does not matter. Sorting on (-score, id) gives highest first with a deterministic tie-break. This exact search is the ground truth an ANN index is measured against.
hints: Build a list of (-score, id) tuples and sort it.
Skip vectors whose norm is 0 to avoid dividing by zero.

tests.name: ties broken by id and zero vectors skipped

coding.title: Recall@k of an ANN index
coding.prompt:
Write `recall_at_k(exact, approx, k)` where `exact` and `approx` are lists of ranked id lists, one per query. For each query, recall is the size of the overlap between the first `k` ids of each list divided by `k`. Return the mean over queries rounded to 3 decimals. Return 0.0 if there are no queries.

Example: `recall_at_k([['a','b']], [['b','c']], 2)` returns `0.5`.
coding.explanation: Order within the top k does not matter for recall, so set intersection is right. Averaging over queries gives the index-level number you compare across ef_search or nprobe settings.
hints: Slice both lists to k before comparing.
Use set intersection to count overlap.
Sum the per-query recalls and divide by the number of queries.

tests.name: only first k counted and empty input

coding.title: Pre-filter versus post-filter
coding.prompt:
Write `post_filter(ranked, meta, tenant, k)` and `pre_filter(ranked_all, meta, tenant, k)`.

- `post_filter` takes only the first `k` ids of `ranked`, then keeps those whose `meta[id] == tenant`.
- `pre_filter` keeps ids matching the tenant from the full ranking `ranked_all` first, then returns up to `k` of them.

Both keep ranking order. Example: with ranking `['a','b','c','d']`, meta `{'a':1,'b':1,'c':2,'d':2}`, tenant 2 and k 2: post returns `[]`, pre returns `['c','d']`.
coding.explanation: The only difference is the order of slicing and filtering. Slicing first (post) can leave nothing for a selective tenant; filtering first (pre) always fills k when enough matches exist. Real engines do the second efficiently inside the index.
hints: The two functions differ only in whether you slice before or after filtering.
Use meta.get(d) so unknown ids do not raise.
post: [d for d in ranked[:k] if ...]; pre: [d for d in ranked_all if ...][:k]

tests.name: order kept and capped at k
